claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The proposed model is a physics-informed neural network incorporating descriptors of inter-scale chemical fluctuations and grain-boundary or heterointerface features.
Targeted high-fidelity fracture simulations and experimental tensile and fracture data will be integrated into model training.
A neural-network-based method can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness-related properties of alloys.
The proposed method can predict fracture toughness specifically for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error by at least approximately 20% relative to conventional ML, CALPHAD, or full first-principles methods.
The proposed model will decrease computational demand or computation time by approximately fivefold.
The intended operating domain is room-temperature tensile and fracture testing of well-characterized hierarchical microstructures.
Refined descriptors can quantify multilevel chemical fluctuations and heterointerfaces in the hierarchical heterostructure.
Embedding elasticity theory and fracture-mechanics constraints into the neural network improves interpolation and extrapolation across elastic loading, yield initiation, and fracture propagation.
Combining high-fidelity simulations with machine learning is an established materials-design approach.
Stand-alone CALPHAD, first-principles simulations, and black-box machine-learning models are computationally expensive.
Existing approaches have limited fracture-toughness accuracy because they insufficiently represent multiscale heterogeneity.
The model's reliability will diminish for microstructures, stress states, temperatures, or chemical fluctuations outside the training and descriptor calibration ranges.
Preliminary studies suggest a 20% accuracy improvement and a fivefold efficiency improvement.
The expected gains may vary with training-data quality, training-data coverage, and heterostructural features omitted from the descriptors.
Young's modulus can be benchmarked using ultrasonic or nanoindentation measurements, yield strength by tensile testing, and fracture toughness by standardized compact-tension testing.
The prospective benchmark will use blinded predictions on newly synthesized HfNbTiVAl10 batches whose microstructures remain within the descriptor range.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if modulus or yield-strength deviations exceed 20%, fracture-toughness deviations exceed 25%, or the speedup is less than fivefold.
